summary: Defines the procedures and extensions to RSVP-TE needed to support unnumbered links in MPLS traffic engineering. The signaling at the time did not support links that have no IP address of their own, which this document addresses.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3477 lets RSVP-TE identify point-to-point links that have no IP address. Routers assign local link numbers and carry those numbers in signaling messages that set up and record an MPLS path.

questions: mpls te links without ip addresses
what is an unnumbered link in mpls
how does rsvp-te signal unnumbered links
what is the lsp tunnel interface id object
subtitle: How RSVP-TE signals MPLS traffic-engineered paths over links without IP addresses.

tldr.problem: RSVP-TE route objects identify links by IP address, so they cannot name an unnumbered link directly.
tldr.mechanism: Each link endpoint assigns a non-zero 32-bit identifier. New ERO and RRO subobjects carry the router ID and interface identifier, and a new RSVP object supports forwarding adjacencies.
tldr.outcome: RSVP-TE can signal and record paths through unnumbered links. RFC 3477 is updated by RFC 6107.

today: RFC 3477 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2003 and is updated by RFC 6107.

sections.title: Naming an Unnumbered Link
sections.content:
MPLS traffic engineering over an unnumbered link needs routing protocols to advertise link information and signaling to identify the link. This document addresses the signaling part; separate extensions cover routing-protocol information.

RSVP-TE previously had no way to name an unnumbered link in an Explicit Route Object (ERO) or Record Route Object (RRO). RFC 3477 adds procedures and message extensions for this purpose.
sections.plainLanguage: RSVP-TE needs a way to refer to a link that has no IP address. This RFC adds identifiers that let routers include those links in a signaled path.

sections.title: Local and Remote Link Identifiers
sections.content:
An unnumbered link must be point-to-point. Each Label Switching Router at an end assigns a non-zero 32-bit identifier that is unique within that router. The two routers do not have to choose the same number.

The routers must learn each other's identifiers. The RFC lists configuration, LMP, RSVP or CR-LDP, and routing-protocol extensions as possible ways to exchange them. A stable Router ID identifies the router independently of a particular interface.
sections.plainLanguage: Each end assigns its own identifier to the link. The routers exchange those identifiers so each can describe the link from its own side.

sections.title: Unnumbered Forwarding Adjacencies
sections.content:
A Forwarding Adjacency is an LSP advertised as a link in IS-IS or OSPF, or used as a component link in a bundle. If it is unnumbered, the headend assigns an identifier and includes an LSP_TUNNEL_INTERFACE_ID object in the Path message.

The tail end also assigns an identifier and returns it in the Resv message. The endpoints then treat the adjacency like another unnumbered link when processing route and hop information.
sections.plainLanguage: A tunnel advertised as a network link also needs an identifier at each end. The Path and Resv messages carry those identifiers between the endpoints.

sections.title: ERO, RRO, and Interface-ID Fields
sections.content:
The LSP_TUNNEL_INTERFACE_ID object has class number 193, C-Type 1, and length 12. It carries a Router ID and a 32-bit Interface ID. In a Path message it is the Forward Interface ID; in a Resv message it is the Reverse Interface ID.

The new Unnumbered Interface ID subobject has type 4 and length 12 in both ERO and RRO contexts. It identifies the router and its local link number; the RRO version also records local protection flags.
sections.plainLanguage: The new fields pair a router's stable identifier with the number it assigned to a link. ERO uses that pair to select a link, and RRO records that the path used it.

sections.title: Processing and Recording the Route
sections.content:
An LSR matches an incoming interface identifier against a link using the tuple of Router ID and local identifier. If it finds no matching link while processing an IF_ID RSVP_HOP object, it should return error code 24 and error value 16.

When the ERO selects an unnumbered outgoing link, the Path message sent to the next hop includes the sender's Router ID and its assigned interface identifier. If a matching RRO is in use, the router appends a subobject recording that link.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router checks whether the router ID and interface number identify one of its links. It reports an error if it cannot find the link and records the link when forwarding the route.

sections.title: Security and Assigned Numbers
sections.content:
The RFC describes this as a small clarification and extension to RSVP-TE and says it poses no new security concerns. It notes that the extra interface identifier might make an RSVP message harder to spoof.

The document defines subobjects for ERO and RRO and requests an RSVP class number for LSP_TUNNEL_INTERFACE_ID. The assigned class number uses a form that lets an unknown object be ignored while forwarded.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC reports no new security concern from the identifier extension. It also defines registry assignments so RSVP implementations can recognize and forward the new information.
